implementation_notes: Default Scala realization on Kafka: the consumer group is the durable subscription, and the committable-offset stream makes acknowledgement order explicit. Choose it in Akka/Pekko systems where catch-up should be backpressured instead of a burst.
code_sketch:
val settings = ConsumerSettings(system, new StringDeserializer, new StringDeserializer)
  .withGroupId("billing-ledger")                       // durable identity
  .withProperty(ConsumerConfig.AUTO_OFFSET_RESET_CONFIG, "earliest")
Consumer.committableSource(settings, Subscriptions.topics("orders"))
  .mapAsync(1)(m => handle(m.record.value()).map(_ => m.committableOffset))
  .toMat(Committer.sink(CommitterSettings(system)))(DrainingControl.apply).run()
pitfalls: DrainingControl must be invoked on shutdown or the stream is killed with uncommitted offsets.
A failing stage stops the stream: without supervision the backlog waits until the stream is restarted.

variants.name: JMS durable subscription through the JVM API
variants.implementation_notes: Where the broker is a JMS provider, Scala uses the Java API unchanged and the provider holds both the subscription record and the backlog, which suits partners that must never miss a published document. Choose it when the subscription lifecycle should be managed by the messaging standard rather than by a log retention policy.
variants.code_sketch:
val sub = session.createDurableSubscriber(topic, "billing-ledger")
sub.setMessageListener(m => { handle(m); m.acknowledge() })
pitfalls: The listener runs on the provider's thread; blocking Scala work there stalls delivery.
Unsubscribe is the only way the backlog stops growing for a retired subscriber.
